Scarce Units, Typed, Related, Actionable.

An open-source, self-hosted ontology platform.
Your data becomes one model you own: typed, linked, changed only through rules the server enforces, and every number traces back to its source.

Quick start · How it works · Proposals · Python SDK · Contributing

Beta. Only small parts are still alpha: the model language and APIs may still change between versions, and parts of the user interface and docs are unfinished.

Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS is a one-person project so far. See Contributing.

Motivation

Sutra-OS began in late 2025 as a thought experiment: a free version of the system described in Ontology-Oriented Software Development, whose creators I deeply admire.

Much talent today goes into software that sells attention, while the software everything else runs on is mostly free: by a rough estimate, 70–90% of US economic output depends on free software at some critical point. That openness is not guaranteed. In November 2026, Nvidia's board parted with the founder who had its AI models released openly. Sutra-OS adds to the commons under the AGPL, so that it stays readable by anyone.

The past ten years have shown what it costs when nobody can see what depends on what. In 2017, NotPetya spread through a single Ukrainian accounting program and stopped Maersk's ports and Merck's factories. In 2023, a corrupted file in one FAA system halted every domestic departure in the US. In 2024, one faulty CrowdStrike update crashed millions of Windows machines, and airlines, hospitals and banks stood still. In November 2026, a single vendor took Outlook down for a day and some cities went back to fax. That same week, data flooded the FAA's telecommunications network, aging routers buckled, and the US saw only the third nationwide ground stop in its history. No one, it seems, had those routers on the map of what keeps planes in the air, so no one could ask beforehand what would stop if they failed.

That question is what Sutra-OS is built for. Every system, device, dataset and decision becomes an object with links to what it feeds and what feeds it, and every number can be traced back to its source. Whoever holds such a model can ask, before the outage, what stops when one piece fails, and get an answer, at every scale from a single person to a government (hopefully never a world government). Many small ontologies, each held by those it describes, keep power spread out; one model of everything would not.

Scarce Units: energy, water, land, housing and time will shape the coming decades. Whoever counts what is scarce decides how it is shared, and today that bookkeeping sits with a few platforms; for most people, the only trace their own data leaves in their life is the tendinitis from the hundredth weary click on "Accept all" in a cookie banner. Sutra-OS keeps the bookkeeping with those it concerns, under rules everyone can read: households, farms, workshops, clubs, newsrooms and public administrations get their records back, and their wrist with them. That is what a democracy needs from its software: a council that can trace the number behind a decision to its source, a change that stays a proposal until someone answers for it, and a public administration accountable to its voters rather than to a vendor under another country's law.

Who it is for

Almost everyone. Whoever you are, someone else keeps a better-connected record of your affairs than you do. Sutra is for anyone who wants their own.

Quick start

Requirements: Linux x86_64, JDK 21, the Clojure CLI, Node.js, Python 3, git.

git clone <repository-url> sutra && cd sutra
(cd clients/frontend && npm install)
bin/sutra-solo

This starts an embedded PostgreSQL and the server on 127.0.0.1 and prints the address. Data lives in $SUTRA_HOME (default ~/.local/share/sutra). The admin password is in zugang.edn ("access") there. Run the bin/sutra bind … line it prints once.

How it works

Three ideas carry the whole platform: object types, link types and action types. The examples below use the farm model in resources/presets.

1. Object types: what is there

You start by saying what exists: a lot of hay, from one field and one cut; a sale, to one buyer. Each is a typed thing with a kind and a key.

:objects
{:lot
 {:name "Hay lot" :plural "Hay lots" :symbol "🌾" :title :name
  :primary-key :name :match-keys [:name]
  :attributes
  [[:name    :string  {:name "Lot"}]                    ; "North Meadow, 1st cut 2026"
   [:baled   :integer {:name "Bales made" :constraints {:min 0}}]
   [:sold    :integer {:derived {:expression [:connected-sum :sales :bales]}}]
   [:in-barn :integer
    {:name "In the barn" :visibility :prominent
     :derived {:language :clojure
               :expression [:- [:get :baled] [:get :sold]]
               :inputs [:baled :sold]}}]]}

 :sale
 {:name "Sale" :symbol "🤝" :primary-key :sale-nr :match-keys [:sale-nr]
  :attributes
  [[:sale-nr        :string]
   [:lot            :string]
   [:buyer          :string]
   [:bales          :integer {:constraints {:min 1}}]
   [:price-per-bale :decimal]
   [:sold-on        :date]
   [:sold-by        :string]]}}

Nobody types or counts :in-barn: it is the bales made minus every bale sold, computed by the server. :bales is an integer, so "about forty" or -3 is refused before anything is written.

An object type is a typed table with a name, a face in the UI and a class in the generated SDK. Properties are typed, constrained and can be derived, so a value nobody typed in still shows up like any other column.

2. Link types: who belongs to whom

A sale on its own is just a number. A sale linked to the lot it came out of is a fact everyone can see.

:links
[[:sale-lot :sale :lot :many-to-one
  {:fk :lot :forward-api-name :lot :reverse-api-name :sales}]]

The sale names its lot and the link follows it: from the lot you see its sales, from a sale its lot, and :connected-sum above sums across that link. One line, and the barn knows what is in it.

Links are first-class: named in both directions, navigable in the UI, traversable in the SDK (lot.sales), and usable in derived values, filters and object sets.

3. Action types: what you're allowed to do

In most systems anybody may change anything, and nobody can say who did. Here there is no "update row". There are only actions: named decisions with typed inputs and rules the server enforces. Selling hay is one of them, and it has a condition.

:sell-hay
{:on     :lot
 :params {:lot            {:type :lot :required true}
          :sale-nr        {:type :string :required true}
          :buyer          {:type :string :required true}
          :bales          {:type :integer :required true :constraints {:min 1}}
          :price-per-bale {:type :decimal}
          :sold-on        {:type :date :prefill :now}
          :sold-by        {:type :string :exposure :hidden :prefill :current-user}}
 :submission-criteria
 [{:message "Not that many bales in the barn."
   :test    {:want [:get :bales] :have [:get :lot :in-barn]}
   :pred    [:<= :want :have]}]
 :rules  [{:op :create :object-type :sale
           :values {:sale-nr [:get :sale-nr] :lot [:get :lot :name]
                    :buyer [:get :buyer] :bales [:get :bales]
                    :price-per-bale [:get :price-per-bale]
                    :sold-on [:get :sold-on] :sold-by [:get :sold-by]}}]
 :edits  [{:object-type :sale}]}

Ask to sell more bales than are in the barn and the server refuses and says why, with the same sentence for the phone, the CLI, the Python script and the AI agent. A refused action writes nothing. Every sale records who made it, and nobody can put someone else's name there.

Actions are the only write path: typed parameters, validation, submission criteria and state transitions, defined once and enforced everywhere.

Every rule you would otherwise keep in your head has this shape: a fact the server computes, and an action that checks it. Declare it once, and stop remembering it.

The same three ideas run the arable side of the farm. A field's margin is derived from its paid harvests and the hay sold off it, two links away. A harvest moves from planted to harvested, delivered and paid only through its actions, and Sell harvest refuses to run without a signed delivery note and a quality test of your own.

Nothing happens until you say so

In most software, deciding and doing are one step. In Sutra they are two. When you sell hay, the server first writes down what would change: one new sale, forty bales, your name on it. Nothing has happened yet. Only when that note is approved does the barn change.

Everything else follows from that:

  • You can always ask first. "Would this work?" is the same question, without the last step.
  • An agent can only make suggestions. What it hands back is the note, never the change. You decide.
  • You can try things out. Run the same decisions on a copy, compare, and keep the real one untouched.
  • You can look back. Every approved change is kept, so last Tuesday's state is still there to read.
  • The answer is the same everywhere. The rule is checked in one place, so the phone, the script and the agent hear the same no.

And it is not a promise. A test fails if the part that decides ever does anything but decide.

More capabilities

  • Your data comes in as it is. Mail over IMAP, CSV exports, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SSH, shaped by transforms in Python, SQL or Clojure.

  • Every number has a past. Lineage runs from each object back through the transforms and datasets to the mail, statement or row it came from (sutra lineage <node>). When someone else's figures disagree with yours, you open the source.

  • Agents get only the tools you name. An action, a function, a query on one type. By default (:writes :propose) their changes are staged as proposals; a rejected one doesn't come back, and the model's prompt and answer are kept with the run.

  • The model is versioned like code. Model and data live on branches. You stage a change, commit it, open a proposal, see who consumes what you touched, and merge into main only when it's reviewed. Webhooks and notifications stay silent on a branch unless you say otherwise.

  • Share exactly what you choose. Markings on types and properties are mandatory access control; grants on projects decide who may read, act and invoke. A group (a co-op, a tenants' association, a family) can pool what its members agree to share, and nothing else, and the server enforces it on every read: lists, filters, counts and totals. One person's data can't show what everyone else was offered. A group's can.

  • Builders and users are different people. One person writes the model; everyone else gets apps with the build tools locked away, and a server that says no when no is the right answer.

  • Secrets stay out of reach. A separate egress agent holds every external credential, so the code that reads your mail never sees the password.

The model as the SDK

You described the farm once. Generate a Python SDK from it, and your code speaks the farm's language: lots, harvests and buyers, and the things you are allowed to do with them, not tables and joins.

pip install ./clients/python-platform-sdk
sutra-platform-sdk generate --base-url http://127.0.0.1:<port> \
                            --username admin --password "…" --out farm_sdk.py

farm_sdk.py is plain, typed Python: a class per object type, an attribute per property and link, a method per action with the action's parameters as its signature. Sutra's language server (clients/ent-lsp) runs pyright for Python and labels each completion as what it is in the model (property, link-type, action, state); any editor that lets you pick the language server can run it (Neovim config).

An action is a method. Its signature comes from the model; a missing argument is flagged before anything runs.

lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025")

lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour")
# error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr"

lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour", sale_nr="S-2026-010")   # ok

States are types. A harvest's status is Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'], so the editor offers exactly those four.

for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests:
    if h.status == "planted":       # completes: planted, harvested, delivered, paid
        h.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)

Filters are checked too. Comparing bales with a string, or reading a link that may be empty, fails in the editor, not on the farm.

Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "forty")   # error: Operator "<" not supported for types
                                   #   "Property[int]" and "Literal['forty']"
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)        # ok

lot.field.margin                   # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"
if lot.field:
    lot.field.margin               # ok
The walkthrough in code: objects with their links, acting, asking first, proposing, lifecycles, server-side aggregates, sets, branches and revisions 
from sutra_platform_sdk import SutraClient, sum_, avg, count, by, bucket
from farm_sdk import Lot, Sale, Field, Buyer, register_all

client = register_all(SutraClient("http://127.0.0.1:<port>", username="admin", password="…"))

An object, not a row. A lot brings its derived values and its links along. Nobody stored in_barn; the server computes it.

lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025")   # a Lot, or NotFound
lot.baled, lot.sold, lot.in_barn            # (120, 95, 25)
lot.field                                   # <Field 'North Meadow'>: the field it was cut from
[(s.buyer, s.bales) for s in lot.sales]     # its three sales, each a Sale

Act on it. Selling hay is something you do to a lot. The server checks the rule, writes the sale, stamps your name on it and tells you what changed.

lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-010", buyer="Neighbour", bales=20, price_per_bale=4.50)
Lot.get(lot.name).in_barn                   # 5

Ask first, or only propose. The same call can be a question (nothing is written) or a proposal (staged until someone approves it). That is how an agent gets to use it.

from sutra_platform_sdk.actions import ActionConfig, ActionMode

ask = ActionConfig(mode=ActionMode.VALIDATE_ONLY)
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=40,
             action_config=ask).validation.submission_criteria
# ('Not that many bales in the barn.',)

lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5,
             publish=False).staged          # True: a proposal, the barn is unchanged

Walk a lifecycle. A harvest goes from planted to harvested, delivered and paid, one action per step, and the rules travel with them. The states are declared in the model, so status is typed Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'] and your editor offers exactly those four.

from datetime import date

wheat = next(h for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests if h.status == "planted")
mill  = Buyer.get("stone-mill")

wheat.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212)
# ServerError: HTTP 422: No signed delivery note. Without one, the buyer decides later what you delivered.
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212, delivery_note=True, quality_tested=True)
Buyer.get("stone-mill").unpaid              # 13038: what the mill owes you, until …
wheat.record_payment()
Field.get("hilltop").margin                 # … the wheat lands in the field's margin

Ask the whole farm, in one line. Who bought how much hay, month by month, at what price. Grouped, summed and sorted on the server; nothing is downloaded to be counted.

Sale.aggregate(
    sum_(Sale.bales), avg(Sale.price_per_bale), count(),
    group_by=[bucket(Sale.sold_on, "month"), by(Sale.buyer)],
    order_by=sum_(Sale.bales), desc=True,
).flat()
# [{'sold_on_month': '2025-12', 'buyer': 'Riding stables', 'bales_sum': 80,
#   'price_per_bale_avg': Decimal('4.5000000000000000'), 'count': 2}, …]

Money stays Decimal all the way from the database; nothing is rounded through a float.

Sets, not lists. On the class, a property is a filter and a link is a hop. Combine sets with |, & and -; the server plans it, and you fetch only what you iterate. Each set knows what it holds: running_low is an ObjectSet[Lot], and one hop along Lot.sales makes it an ObjectSet[Sale].

running_low = Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)
neighbours  = Sale.where(Sale.buyer == "Neighbour").around(Sale.lot)

(running_low - neighbours).count()          # 3: running low, and the neighbour never bought from them
running_low.around(Lot.sales).aggregate(sum_(Sale.bales), group_by=[by(Sale.buyer)])   # who emptied them

Try tomorrow's rule on today's farm, or look at last Tuesday. Everything above runs unchanged against a branch, and every action tells you the revision it landed in, a state you can read again later.

with client.branch("new-rule"):             # made with: sutra branch new-rule
    lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-012", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5)   # main never notices

sale = lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-013", buyer="Neighbour", bales=1)
client.at(sale.revision).objects("sale")    # the sales as they stood right then

And what it refuses. Wrong names, missing arguments and wrong types fail in your editor, before anything runs. Broken rules fail on the server, with the same sentence for every client. If the model changes underneath you, register_all refuses to run until you regenerate.

lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour")   # error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr"
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-1", buyer="Neighbour", bales="20")
                                            # error: "Literal['20']" is not assignable to "int"
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "about forty")      # error: Operator "<" not supported for types
                                            #   "Property[int]" and "Literal['about forty']"
lot.field.margin                            # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"

These are pyright's messages against the generated farm SDK. The SDK's tests run the same lines through pyright, against an SDK generated from a schema captured from a running server, not from a hand-written imitation of one.

None of this is a reporting layer bolted on afterwards. The UI, the CLI, the REST API and the agents ask the same questions and take the same actions through the same door, which is why an agent can be handed Lot and sell_hay and nothing else.

Development

./bin/start.sh   # backend + shadow-cljs watch; PostgreSQL from SUTRA_PG_URL
./bin/stop.sh
(cd tests/frontend && npm install)   # once: the browser tests' driver (playwright-core)
bin/test         # full suite; integration tiers start PostgreSQL in podman
Path What lives there
src/ the server
libs/ libraries the server, the clients and the tests share: kernel (reference interpreter), world (the world as a db value), commits, service, dialect, core, lib (the .ent dialect as a library), calx, store, store-pg
clients/ frontend, CLI, language server, Python SDK, and the babashka tools behind bin/change and bin/enta
plugins/ optional modules (SSO, LLM, packages, …)
boundaries/ the published interfaces, conformance kits and their register (resources/sutra/boundaries.edn), Apache-2.0
resources/ the .ent grammar and example models (presets), platform config, the web client's static files
distributions/ ready-to-run bundles (sutra-solo)
tests/ backend suites, the scenario, and tests/frontend
bin/ start, stop, test and tooling scripts

The semantics are pinned by an executable scenario, an aircraft maintenance shop in tests/scenario: "no release while a defect is open" is the barn rule above in another world.

Security: set SUTRA_HTTP_BIND when running the plain server (it defaults to 0.0.0.0). ./bin/start.sh allows anonymous access, so never expose it. Transforms run user code on the server, so grant that right accordingly.

Contributing

Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS needs people who will take responsibility for part of it over time: the server, the web client, the Python SDK, connectors, packaging and installation, docs, or the example models. You don't need to know all of it. Start with a few contributions in one area; if you'd like to stay, say so in an issue.

The most useful contributions are not always code:

  • A model for an everyday problem. A tenancy, a pension, a medical bill, a small association's membership. If a rule protects someone, it belongs in resources/presets.
  • Plain-language guides for the person who sets Sutra up for others.
  • Translations. Parts of the code base and the examples are in German; the user interface should speak more languages than two.
  • Code. Send a failing test or a fix.

Open an issue for questions, ideas and bug reports. Be kind: the person on the other side may be the one this was built for.

The code is offered as is, in the spirit of Rich Hickey's Open Source is Not About You: nobody is owed a feature, a fix or an answer, and that includes the maintainers. What keeps it going is people choosing to help.

Acknowledgements

The ontology model of objects, links and actions follows the one popularised by Palantir Foundry; Sutra-OS was built from its public documentation. The web client is built on Palantir's Blueprint UI toolkit (Apache-2.0), vendored as a ClojureScript port in clients/frontend/vendor/blueprint-cljs. The implementation owes everything to Rich Hickey and Clojure, and to his almost spiritual talk Are We There Yet?, which will perhaps continue to transform the software craft into eternity. Claude Code wrote all of the code.

License

AGPL-3.0-or-later, with a section 7 exception for linking with EPL libraries such as Clojure. See LICENSE. The AGPL means anyone who runs a modified Sutra as a service for others must offer them the source, so the tool stays in the hands of the people it serves.

No patent search has been carried out. The AGPL licenses contributors' patents only; checking third-party patents where they apply is up to you. Palantir and Foundry are trademarks of Palantir Technologies Inc.; Sutra-OS is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by Palantir.

Selling hay is one of them, and it has a condition. :sell-hay {:on :lot :params {:lot {:type :lot :required true} :sale-nr {:type :string :required true} :buyer {:type :string :required true} :bales {:type :integer :required true :constraints {:min 1}} :price-per-bale {:type :decimal} :sold-on {:type :date :prefill :now} :sold-by {:type :string :exposure :hidden :prefill :current-user}} :submission-criteria [{:message "Not that many bales in the barn." :test {:want [:get :bales] :have [:get :lot :in-barn]} :pred [:<= :want :have]}] :rules [{:op :create :object-type :sale :values {:sale-nr [:get :sale-nr] :lot [:get :lot :name] :buyer [:get :buyer] :bales [:get :bales] :price-per-bale [:get :price-per-bale] :sold-on [:get :sold-on] :sold-by [:get :sold-by]}}] :edits [{:object-type :sale}]} Ask to sell more bales than are in the barn and the server refuses and says why, with the same sentence for the phone, the CLI, the Python script and the AI agent. A refused action writes nothing. Every sale records who made it, and nobody can put someone else's name there. Actions are the only write path: typed parameters, validation, submission criteria and state transitions, defined once and enforced everywhere. Every rule you would otherwise keep in your head has this shape: a fact the server computes, and an action that checks it. Declare it once, and stop remembering it. The same three ideas run the arable side of the farm. A field's margin is derived from its paid harvests and the hay sold off it, two links away. A harvest moves from planted to harvested, delivered and paid only through its actions, and Sell harvest refuses to run without a signed delivery note and a quality test of your own. Nothing happens until you say so In most software, deciding and doing are one step. In Sutra they are two. When you sell hay, the server first writes down what would change: one new sale, forty bales, your name on it. Nothing has happened yet. Only when that note is approved does the barn change. Everything else follows from that: You can always ask first. "Would this work?" is the same question, without the last step. An agent can only make suggestions. What it hands back is the note, never the change. You decide. You can try things out. Run the same decisions on a copy, compare, and keep the real one untouched. You can look back. Every approved change is kept, so last Tuesday's state is still there to read. The answer is the same everywhere. The rule is checked in one place, so the phone, the script and the agent hear the same no. And it is not a promise. A test fails if the part that decides ever does anything but decide. More capabilities Your data comes in as it is. Mail over IMAP, CSV exports, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SSH, shaped by transforms in Python, SQL or Clojure. Every number has a past. Lineage runs from each object back through the transforms and datasets to the mail, statement or row it came from (sutra lineage <node>). When someone else's figures disagree with yours, you open the source. Agents get only the tools you name. An action, a function, a query on one type. By default (:writes :propose) their changes are staged as proposals; a rejected one doesn't come back, and the model's prompt and answer are kept with the run. The model is versioned like code. Model and data live on branches. You stage a change, commit it, open a proposal, see who consumes what you touched, and merge into main only when it's reviewed. Webhooks and notifications stay silent on a branch unless you say otherwise. Share exactly what you choose. Markings on types and properties are mandatory access control; grants on projects decide who may read, act and invoke. A group (a co-op, a tenants' association, a family) can pool what its members agree to share, and nothing else, and the server enforces it on every read: lists, filters, counts and totals. One person's data can't show what everyone else was offered. A group's can. Builders and users are different people. One person writes the model; everyone else gets apps with the build tools locked away, and a server that says no when no is the right answer. Secrets stay out of reach. A separate egress agent holds every external credential, so the code that reads your mail never sees the password. The model as the SDK You described the farm once. Generate a Python SDK from it, and your code speaks the farm's language: lots, harvests and buyers, and the things you are allowed to do with them, not tables and joins. pip install ./clients/python-platform-sdk sutra-platform-sdk generate --base-url http://127.0.0.1:<port> \ --username admin --password "…" --out farm_sdk.py farm_sdk.py is plain, typed Python: a class per object type, an attribute per property and link, a method per action with the action's parameters as its signature. Sutra's language server (clients/ent-lsp) runs pyright for Python and labels each completion as what it is in the model (property, link-type, action, state); any editor that lets you pick the language server can run it (Neovim config). An action is a method. Its signature comes from the model; a missing argument is flagged before anything runs. lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025") lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour") # error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr" lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour", sale_nr="S-2026-010") # ok States are types. A harvest's status is Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'], so the editor offers exactly those four. for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests: if h.status == "planted": # completes: planted, harvested, delivered, paid h.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5) Filters are checked too. Comparing bales with a string, or reading a link that may be empty, fails in the editor, not on the farm. Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "forty") # error: Operator "<" not supported for types # "Property[int]" and "Literal['forty']" Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50) # ok lot.field.margin # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None" if lot.field: lot.field.margin # ok The walkthrough in code: objects with their links, acting, asking first, proposing, lifecycles, server-side aggregates, sets, branches and revisions from sutra_platform_sdk import SutraClient, sum_, avg, count, by, bucket from farm_sdk import Lot, Sale, Field, Buyer, register_all client = register_all(SutraClient("http://127.0.0.1:<port>", username="admin", password="…")) An object, not a row. A lot brings its derived values and its links along. Nobody stored in_barn; the server computes it. lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025") # a Lot, or NotFound lot.baled, lot.sold, lot.in_barn # (120, 95, 25) lot.field # <Field 'North Meadow'>: the field it was cut from [(s.buyer, s.bales) for s in lot.sales] # its three sales, each a Sale Act on it. Selling hay is something you do to a lot. The server checks the rule, writes the sale, stamps your name on it and tells you what changed. lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-010", buyer="Neighbour", bales=20, price_per_bale=4.50) Lot.get(lot.name).in_barn # 5 Ask first, or only propose. The same call can be a question (nothing is written) or a proposal (staged until someone approves it). That is how an agent gets to use it. from sutra_platform_sdk.actions import ActionConfig, ActionMode ask = ActionConfig(mode=ActionMode.VALIDATE_ONLY) lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=40, action_config=ask).validation.submission_criteria # ('Not that many bales in the barn.',) lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5, publish=False).staged # True: a proposal, the barn is unchanged Walk a lifecycle. A harvest goes from planted to harvested, delivered and paid, one action per step, and the rules travel with them. The states are declared in the model, so status is typed Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'] and your editor offers exactly those four. from datetime import date wheat = next(h for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests if h.status == "planted") mill = Buyer.get("stone-mill") wheat.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5) wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212) # ServerError: HTTP 422: No signed delivery note. Without one, the buyer decides later what you delivered. wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212, delivery_note=True, quality_tested=True) Buyer.get("stone-mill").unpaid # 13038: what the mill owes you, until … wheat.record_payment() Field.get("hilltop").margin # … the wheat lands in the field's margin Ask the whole farm, in one line. Who bought how much hay, month by month, at what price. Grouped, summed and sorted on the server; nothing is downloaded to be counted. Sale.aggregate( sum_(Sale.bales), avg(Sale.price_per_bale), count(), group_by=[bucket(Sale.sold_on, "month"), by(Sale.buyer)], order_by=sum_(Sale.bales), desc=True, ).flat() # [{'sold_on_month': '2025-12', 'buyer': 'Riding stables', 'bales_sum': 80, # 'price_per_bale_avg': Decimal('4.5000000000000000'), 'count': 2}, …] Money stays Decimal all the way from the database; nothing is rounded through a float. Sets, not lists. On the class, a property is a filter and a link is a hop. Combine sets with |, & and -; the server plans it, and you fetch only what you iterate. Each set knows what it holds: running_low is an ObjectSet[Lot], and one hop along Lot.sales makes it an ObjectSet[Sale]. running_low = Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50) neighbours = Sale.where(Sale.buyer == "Neighbour").around(Sale.lot) (running_low - neighbours).count() # 3: running low, and the neighbour never bought from them running_low.around(Lot.sales).aggregate(sum_(Sale.bales), group_by=[by(Sale.buyer)]) # who emptied them Try tomorrow's rule on today's farm, or look at last Tuesday. Everything above runs unchanged against a branch, and every action tells you the revision it landed in, a state you can read again later. with client.branch("new-rule"): # made with: sutra branch new-rule lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-012", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5) # main never notices sale = lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-013", buyer="Neighbour", bales=1) client.at(sale.revision).objects("sale") # the sales as they stood right then And what it refuses. Wrong names, missing arguments and wrong types fail in your editor, before anything runs. Broken rules fail on the server, with the same sentence for every client. If the model changes underneath you, register_all refuses to run until you regenerate. lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour") # error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr" lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-1", buyer="Neighbour", bales="20") # error: "Literal['20']" is not assignable to "int" Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "about forty") # error: Operator "<" not supported for types # "Property[int]" and "Literal['about forty']" lot.field.margin # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None" These are pyright's messages against the generated farm SDK. The SDK's tests run the same lines through pyright, against an SDK generated from a schema captured from a running server, not from a hand-written imitation of one. None of this is a reporting layer bolted on afterwards. The UI, the CLI, the REST API and the agents ask the same questions and take the same actions through the same door, which is why an agent can be handed Lot and sell_hay and nothing else. Development ./bin/start.sh # backend + shadow-cljs watch; PostgreSQL from SUTRA_PG_URL ./bin/stop.sh (cd tests/frontend && npm install) # once: the browser tests' driver (playwright-core) bin/test # full suite; integration tiers start PostgreSQL in podman Path What lives there src/ the server libs/ libraries the server, the clients and the tests share: kernel (reference interpreter), world (the world as a db value), commits, service, dialect, core, lib (the .ent dialect as a library), calx, store, store-pg clients/ frontend, CLI, language server, Python SDK, and the babashka tools behind bin/change and bin/enta plugins/ optional modules (SSO, LLM, packages, …) boundaries/ the published interfaces, conformance kits and their register (resources/sutra/boundaries.edn), Apache-2.0 resources/ the .ent grammar and example models (presets), platform config, the web client's static files distributions/ ready-to-run bundles (sutra-solo) tests/ backend suites, the scenario, and tests/frontend bin/ start, stop, test and tooling scripts The semantics are pinned by an executable scenario, an aircraft maintenance shop in tests/scenario: "no release while a defect is open" is the barn rule above in another world. Security: set SUTRA_HTTP_BIND when running the plain server (it defaults to 0.0.0.0). ./bin/start.sh allows anonymous access, so never expose it. Transforms run user code on the server, so grant that right accordingly. Contributing Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS needs people who will take responsibility for part of it over time: the server, the web client, the Python SDK, connectors, packaging and installation, docs, or the example models. You don't need to know all of it. Start with a few contributions in one area; if you'd like to stay, say so in an issue. The most useful contributions are not always code: A model for an everyday problem. A tenancy, a pension, a medical bill, a small association's membership. If a rule protects someone, it belongs in resources/presets. Plain-language guides for the person who sets Sutra up for others. Translations. Parts of the code base and the examples are in German; the user interface should speak more languages than two. Code. Send a failing test or a fix. Open an issue for questions, ideas and bug reports. Be kind: the person on the other side may be the one this was built for. The code is offered as is, in the spirit of Rich Hickey's Open Source is Not About You: nobody is owed a feature, a fix or an answer, and that includes the maintainers. What keeps it going is people choosing to help. content_html_zh:
Scarce Units, Typed, Related, Actionable.

An open-source, self-hosted ontology platform. Your data becomes one model you own: typed, linked, changed only through rules the server enforces, and every number traces back to its source.

Quick start · How it works · Proposals · Python SDK · Contributing

Beta. Only small parts are still alpha: the model language and APIs may still change between versions, and parts of the user interface and docs are unfinished.
Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS is a one-person project so far. See Contributing.

动机

Sutra-OS began in late 2025 as a thought experiment: a free version of the system described in Ontology-Oriented Software Development, whose creators I deeply admire.

Much talent today goes into software that sells attention, while the software everything else runs on is mostly free: by a rough estimate, 70–90% of US economic output depends on free software at some critical point. That openness is not guaranteed. In November 2026, Nvidia's board parted with the founder who had its AI models released openly. Sutra-OS adds to the commons under the AGPL, so that it stays readable by anyone.

The past ten years have shown what it costs when nobody can see what depends on what. In 2017, NotPetya spread through a single Ukrainian accounting program and stopped Maersk's ports and Merck's factories. In 2023, a corrupted file in one FAA system halted every domestic departure in the US. In 2024, one faulty CrowdStrike update crashed millions of Windows machines, and airlines, hospitals and banks stood still. In November 2026, a single vendor took Outlook down for a day and some cities went back to fax. That same week, data flooded the FAA's telecommunications network, aging routers buckled, and the US saw only the third nationwide ground stop in its history. No one, it seems, had those routers on the map of what keeps planes in the air, so no one could ask beforehand what would stop if they failed.

That question is what Sutra-OS is built for. Every system, device, dataset and decision becomes an object with links to what it feeds and what feeds it, and every number can be traced back to its source. Whoever holds such a model can ask, before the outage, what stops when one piece fails, and get an answer, at every scale from a single person to a government (hopefully never a world government). Many small ontologies, each held by those it describes, keep power spread out; one model of everything would not.

Scarce Units: energy, water, land, housing and time will shape the coming decades. Whoever counts what is scarce decides how it is shared, and today that bookkeeping sits with a few platforms; for most people, the only trace their own data leaves in their life is the tendinitis from the hundredth weary click on "Accept all" in a cookie banner. Sutra-OS keeps the bookkeeping with those it concerns, under rules everyone can read: households, farms, workshops, clubs, newsrooms and public administrations get their records back, and their wrist with them. That is what a democracy needs from its software: a council that can trace the number behind a decision to its source, a change that stays a proposal until someone answers for it, and a public administration accountable to its voters rather than to a vendor under another country's law.

Who it is for

Almost everyone. Whoever you are, someone else keeps a better-connected record of your affairs than you do. Sutra is for anyone who wants their own.

快速启动

Requirements: Linux x86_64, JDK 21, the Clojure CLI, Node.js, Python 3, git.

git clone <repository-url> sutra && cd sutra
(cd clients/frontend && npm install)
bin/sutra-solo

This starts an embedded PostgreSQL and the server on 127.0.0.1 and prints the address. Data lives in $SUTRA_HOME (default ~/.local/share/sutra). The admin password is in zugang.edn ("access") there. Run the bin/sutra bind … line it prints once.

它是如何运作的

Three ideas carry the whole platform: object types, link types and action types. The examples below use the farm model in resources/presets.

1. Object types: what is there

You start by saying what exists: a lot of hay, from one field and one cut; a sale, to one buyer. Each is a typed thing with a kind and a key.

:objects
{:lot
 {:name "Hay lot" :plural "Hay lots" :symbol "🌾" :title :name
  :primary-key :name :match-keys [:name]
  :attributes
  [[:name    :string  {:name "Lot"}]                    ; "North Meadow, 1st cut 2026"
   [:baled   :integer {:name "Bales made" :constraints {:min 0}}]
   [:sold    :integer {:derived {:expression [:connected-sum :sales :bales]}}]
   [:in-barn :integer
    {:name "In the barn" :visibility :prominent
     :derived {:language :clojure
               :expression [:- [:get :baled] [:get :sold]]
               :inputs [:baled :sold]}}]]}

 :sale
 {:name "Sale" :symbol "🤝" :primary-key :sale-nr :match-keys [:sale-nr]
  :attributes
  [[:sale-nr        :string]
   [:lot            :string]
   [:buyer          :string]
   [:bales          :integer {:constraints {:min 1}}]
   [:price-per-bale :decimal]
   [:sold-on        :date]
   [:sold-by        :string]]}}

Nobody types or counts :in-barn: it is the bales made minus every bale sold, computed by the server. :bales is an integer, so "about forty" or -3 is refused before anything is written.

An object type is a typed table with a name, a face in the UI and a class in the generated SDK. Properties are typed, constrained and can be derived, so a value nobody typed in still shows up like any other column.

2. Link types: who belongs to whom

A sale on its own is just a number. A sale linked to the lot it came out of is a fact everyone can see.

:links
[[:sale-lot :sale :lot :many-to-one
  {:fk :lot :forward-api-name :lot :reverse-api-name :sales}]]

The sale names its lot and the link follows it: from the lot you see its sales, from a sale its lot, and :connected-sum above sums across that link. One line, and the barn knows what is in it.

Links are first-class: named in both directions, navigable in the UI, traversable in the SDK (lot.sales), and usable in derived values, filters and object sets.

3. Action types: what you're allowed to do

In most systems anybody may change anything, and nobody can say who did. Here there is no "update row". There are only actions: named decisions with typed inputs and rules the server enforces. Selling hay is one of them, and it has a condition.

:sell-hay
{:on     :lot
 :params {:lot            {:type :lot :required true}
          :sale-nr        {:type :string :required true}
          :buyer          {:type :string :required true}
          :bales          {:type :integer :required true :constraints {:min 1}}
          :price-per-bale {:type :decimal}
          :sold-on        {:type :date :prefill :now}
          :sold-by        {:type :string :exposure :hidden :prefill :current-user}}
 :submission-criteria
 [{:message "Not that many bales in the barn."
   :test    {:want [:get :bales] :have [:get :lot :in-barn]}
   :pred    [:<= :want :have]}]
 :rules  [{:op :create :object-type :sale
           :values {:sale-nr [:get :sale-nr] :lot [:get :lot :name]
                    :buyer [:get :buyer] :bales [:get :bales]
                    :price-per-bale [:get :price-per-bale]
                    :sold-on [:get :sold-on] :sold-by [:get :sold-by]}}]
 :edits  [{:object-type :sale}]}

Ask to sell more bales than are in the barn and the server refuses and says why, with the same sentence for the phone, the CLI, the Python script and the AI agent. A refused action writes nothing. Every sale records who made it, and nobody can put someone else's name there.

Actions are the only write path: typed parameters, validation, submission criteria and state transitions, defined once and enforced everywhere.

Every rule you would otherwise keep in your head has this shape: a fact the server computes, and an action that checks it. Declare it once, and stop remembering it.

The same three ideas run the arable side of the farm. A field's margin is derived from its paid harvests and the hay sold off it, two links away. A harvest moves from planted to harvested, delivered and paid only through its actions, and Sell harvest refuses to run without a signed delivery note and a quality test of your own.

Nothing happens until you say so

In most software, deciding and doing are one step. In Sutra they are two. When you sell hay, the server first writes down what would change: one new sale, forty bales, your name on it. Nothing has happened yet. Only when that note is approved does the barn change.

Everything else follows from that:

  • You can always ask first. "Would this work?" is the same question, without the last step.
  • An agent can only make suggestions. What it hands back is the note, never the change. 你决定。
  • You can try things out. Run the same decisions on a copy, compare, and keep the real one untouched.
  • You can look back. Every approved change is kept, so last Tuesday's state is still there to read.
  • The answer is the same everywhere. The rule is checked in one place, so the phone, the script and the agent hear the same no.

And it is not a promise. A test fails if the part that decides ever does anything but decide.

More capabilities

  • Your data comes in as it is. Mail over IMAP, CSV exports, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SSH, shaped by transforms in Python, SQL or Clojure.
  • Every number has a past. Lineage runs from each object back through the transforms and datasets to the mail, statement or row it came from (sutra lineage <node>). When someone else's figures disagree with yours, you open the source.
  • Agents get only the tools you name. An action, a function, a query on one type. By default (:writes :propose) their changes are staged as proposals; a rejected one doesn't come back, and the model's prompt and answer are kept with the run.
  • The model is versioned like code. Model and data live on branches. You stage a change, commit it, open a proposal, see who consumes what you touched, and merge into main only when it's reviewed. Webhooks and notifications stay silent on a branch unless you say otherwise.
  • Share exactly what you choose. Markings on types and properties are mandatory access control; grants on projects decide who may read, act and invoke. A group (a co-op, a tenants' association, a family) can pool what its members agree to share, and nothing else, and the server enforces it on every read: lists, filters, counts and totals. One person's data can't show what everyone else was offered. A group's can.
  • Builders and users are different people. One person writes the model; everyone else gets apps with the build tools locked away, and a server that says no when no is the right answer.
  • Secrets stay out of reach. A separate egress agent holds every external credential, so the code that reads your mail never sees the password.

The model as the SDK

You described the farm once. Generate a Python SDK from it, and your code speaks the farm's language: lots, harvests and buyers, and the things you are allowed to do with them, not tables and joins.

pip install ./clients/python-platform-sdk
sutra-platform-sdk generate --base-url http://127.0.0.1:<port> \
                            --username admin --password "…" --out farm_sdk.py

farm_sdk.py is plain, typed Python: a class per object type, an attribute per property and link, a method per action with the action's parameters as its signature. Sutra's language server (clients/ent-lsp) runs pyright for Python and labels each completion as what it is in the model (property, link-type, action, state); any editor that lets you pick the language server can run it (Neovim config).

An action is a method. Its signature comes from the model; a missing argument is flagged before anything runs.

lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025")

lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour")
# error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr"

lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour", sale_nr="S-2026-010")   # ok

States are types. A harvest's status is Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'], so the editor offers exactly those four.

for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests:
    if h.status == "planted":       # completes: planted, harvested, delivered, paid
        h.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)

Filters are checked too. Comparing bales with a string, or reading a link that may be empty, fails in the editor, not on the farm.

Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "forty")   # error: Operator "<" not supported for types
                                   #   "Property[int]" and "Literal['forty']"
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)        # ok

lot.field.margin                   # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"
if lot.field:
    lot.field.margin               # ok
The walkthrough in code: objects with their links, acting, asking first, proposing, lifecycles, server-side aggregates, sets, branches and revisions 
from sutra_platform_sdk import SutraClient, sum_, avg, count, by, bucket
from farm_sdk import Lot, Sale, Field, Buyer, register_all

client = register_all(SutraClient("http://127.0.0.1:<port>", username="admin", password="…"))

An object, not a row. A lot brings its derived values and its links along. Nobody stored in_barn; the server computes it.

lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025")   # a Lot, or NotFound
lot.baled, lot.sold, lot.in_barn            # (120, 95, 25)
lot.field                                   # <Field 'North Meadow'>: the field it was cut from
[(s.buyer, s.bales) for s in lot.sales]     # its three sales, each a Sale

Act on it. Selling hay is something you do to a lot. The server checks the rule, writes the sale, stamps your name on it and tells you what changed.

lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-010", buyer="Neighbour", bales=20, price_per_bale=4.50)
Lot.get(lot.name).in_barn                   # 5

Ask first, or only propose. The same call can be a question (nothing is written) or a proposal (staged until someone approves it). That is how an agent gets to use it.

from sutra_platform_sdk.actions import ActionConfig, ActionMode

ask = ActionConfig(mode=ActionMode.VALIDATE_ONLY)
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=40,
             action_config=ask).validation.submission_criteria
# ('Not that many bales in the barn.',)

lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5,
             publish=False).staged          # True: a proposal, the barn is unchanged

Walk a lifecycle. A harvest goes from planted to harvested, delivered and paid, one action per step, and the rules travel with them. The states are declared in the model, so status is typed Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'] and your editor offers exactly those four.

from datetime import date

wheat = next(h for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests if h.status == "planted")
mill  = Buyer.get("stone-mill")

wheat.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212)
# ServerError: HTTP 422: No signed delivery note. Without one, the buyer decides later what you delivered.
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212, delivery_note=True, quality_tested=True)
Buyer.get("stone-mill").unpaid              # 13038: what the mill owes you, until …
wheat.record_payment()
Field.get("hilltop").margin                 # … the wheat lands in the field's margin

Ask the whole farm, in one line. Who bought how much hay, month by month, at what price. Grouped, summed and sorted on the server; nothing is downloaded to be counted.

Sale.aggregate(
    sum_(Sale.bales), avg(Sale.price_per_bale), count(),
    group_by=[bucket(Sale.sold_on, "month"), by(Sale.buyer)],
    order_by=sum_(Sale.bales), desc=True,
).flat()
# [{'sold_on_month': '2025-12', 'buyer': 'Riding stables', 'bales_sum': 80,
#   'price_per_bale_avg': Decimal('4.5000000000000000'), 'count': 2}, …]

Money stays Decimal all the way from the database; nothing is rounded through a float.

Sets, not lists. On the class, a property is a filter and a link is a hop. Combine sets with |, & and -; the server plans it, and you fetch only what you iterate. Each set knows what it holds: running_low is an ObjectSet[Lot], and one hop along Lot.sales makes it an ObjectSet[Sale].

running_low = Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)
neighbours  = Sale.where(Sale.buyer == "Neighbour").around(Sale.lot)

(running_low - neighbours).count()          # 3: running low, and the neighbour never bought from them
running_low.around(Lot.sales).aggregate(sum_(Sale.bales), group_by=[by(Sale.buyer)])   # who emptied them

Try tomorrow's rule on today's farm, or look at last Tuesday. Everything above runs unchanged against a branch, and every action tells you the revision it landed in, a state you can read again later.

with client.branch("new-rule"):             # made with: sutra branch new-rule
    lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-012", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5)   # main never notices

sale = lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-013", buyer="Neighbour", bales=1)
client.at(sale.revision).objects("sale")    # the sales as they stood right then

And what it refuses. Wrong names, missing arguments and wrong types fail in your editor, before anything runs. Broken rules fail on the server, with the same sentence for every client. If the model changes underneath you, register_all refuses to run until you regenerate.

lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour")   # error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr"
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-1", buyer="Neighbour", bales="20")
                                            # error: "Literal['20']" is not assignable to "int"
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "about forty")      # error: Operator "<" not supported for types
                                            #   "Property[int]" and "Literal['about forty']"
lot.field.margin                            # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"

These are pyright's messages against the generated farm SDK. The SDK's tests run the same lines through pyright, against an SDK generated from a schema captured from a running server, not from a hand-written imitation of one.

None of this is a reporting layer bolted on afterwards. The UI, the CLI, the REST API and the agents ask the same questions and take the same actions through the same door, which is why an agent can be handed Lot and sell_hay and nothing else.

贡献

Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS needs people who will take responsibility for part of it over time: the server, the web client, the Python SDK, connectors, packaging and installation, docs, or the example models. You don't need to know all of it. Start with a few contributions in one area; if you'd like to stay, say so in an issue.

The most useful contributions are not always code:

  • A model for an everyday problem. A tenancy, a pension, a medical bill, a small association's membership. If a rule protects someone, it belongs in resources/presets.
  • Plain-language guides for the person who sets Sutra up for others.
  • Translations. Parts of the code base and the examples are in German; the user interface should speak more languages than two.
  • Code. Send a failing test or a fix.

Open an issue for questions, ideas and bug reports. Be kind: the person on the other side may be the one this was built for.

The code is offered as is, in the spirit of Rich Hickey's Open Source is Not About You: nobody is owed a feature, a fix or an answer, and that includes the maintainers. What keeps it going is people choosing to help.
